artiest/olivia-rodrigo.text:
Olivia Rodrigo was born in 2003 in Murrieta, California, and grew up in nearby Temecula. Her father has Filipino roots. At home she heard the alternative rock her parents loved, such as No Doubt, Pearl Jam, The White Stripes and Green Day. She had singing lessons from an early age, began piano at nine and played guitar at twelve. She first became known as an actress, in the Disney series Bizaardvark and High School Musical: The Musical: The Series.

In 2020 she signed with Geffen Records. In early 2021 drivers license was released, a piano ballad about heartbreak that reached number 1 in the United States. good 4 u followed, a song with fast guitars that harks back to the pop-punk of the 2000s. Both were on her debut album Sour (2021), which topped the Billboard 200. Rodrigo writes her own songs, with honest, personal lyrics about growing up, jealousy and insecurity. She alternates restrained ballads with raw rock songs.

With Guts (2023) and You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love (2026), the success continued. She became the first artist whose lead single from each of her first three albums entered directly at number 1. She won three Grammys, and in 2021 Time named her Entertainer of the Year. Rodrigo showed a new generation that guitars and rock influences still belong in pop music.
artiest/olivia-rodrigo.listen: Listen to drivers license and follow how the song begins with just piano and a soft voice. Notice how it grows fuller and louder in the middle section, as the sadness turns into anger.

artiest/olivier-messiaen.text: Olivier Messiaen was for more than sixty years organist of the Église de la Trinité in Paris and a deeply devout Catholic. He built his music on his own modes, on rhythms from India and ancient Greece and on birdsong, which he notated meticulously. He wrote his Quatuor pour la fin du temps as a prisoner of war in a camp near Görlitz, where it was first heard in January 1941. As a teacher he trained, among others, Boulez, Stockhausen and Xenakis.
artiest/olivier-messiaen.listen: Listen to Louange à l'éternité de Jésus and hear how the cello plays an endlessly slow melody above soft, throbbing piano chords.

artiest/omar-bashir.text:
Omar Bashir is an Iraqi-Hungarian musician who plays the oud. He was born in 1970 in Budapest, the son of Munir Bashir, who is widely regarded as one of the greatest virtuosos in the history of the oud and as a master of the modal tradition of the Arabic maqam. His uncle Jamil Bashir was also a well-known oud player. At the age of five he began playing together with his father, after the family had moved to Baghdad, and at nine he played a first solo of a quarter of an hour. Later he taught at the Baghdad Music and Ballet School and founded the ensemble Al Bayariq, with twenty-four musicians.

In 1991 he returned to Budapest and studied classical guitar and Western-oriented music at the Franz Liszt Academy. He played with his father until the latter's death in 1997, including in the widely praised duet Duo de Oud. In 1997 he formed the Omar Bashir Trio with the Hungarian guitarists Andreas and Bálint Petz. His albums include Duo de 'ûd from 1998, Zykrayati in 1999, Flamenco Night in 2000, Al Andalous in 2001, Latin Oud in 2007 and Taqâsîm in 2012. He travelled the world and performed in the Middle East and North America.

His music combines traditional Arabic music and improvisation with influences from jazz, flamenco and Hungarian Roma music. As heir to the Bashir family, he sees himself as one of the last bearers of his family's music. In this way he connects a centuries-old oud tradition with the music of today.
artiest/omar-bashir.listen: Listen to a track from Duo de 'ûd and notice the oud: the sound of the strings and the way it lets a melody float and ornaments it. Ask yourself how improvisation sounds here, compared with jazz.

artiest/one-direction.text:
One Direction was an English-Irish boy band, formed in 2010 in London during the British television programme The X Factor. The members were Niall Horan, Liam Payne, Harry Styles, Louis Tomlinson and Zayn Malik. Both judge Simon Cowell and guest judge Nicole Scherzinger claimed that the idea for the group was theirs. One Direction finished third in the competition and signed with Syco, Cowell's label.

The first single, What Makes You Beautiful, reached number 1 in England. With the debut album Up All Night (2011) they became the first British group whose debut entered at number 1 in America. Take Me Home (2012), Midnight Memories (2013) and Four (2014) also topped the chart there. Social media played a major role in their worldwide success, and the hysteria among fans was often compared with Beatlemania. The Where We Are Tour (2014) grossed some 290 million dollars. The group sold more than 70 million records.

In March 2015 Malik left; with four members, Made in the A.M. (2015) was still released. In January 2016 the group went on indefinite hiatus, and all the members began solo careers. Harry Styles had a worldwide hit in 2022 with As It Was. Liam Payne died in October 2024 after a fall from a hotel balcony in Buenos Aires. One Direction shows how the old recipe of the boy band, young singers brought together by a producer and a TV show, could work even more strongly in the age of social media.
artiest/one-direction.listen: In What Makes You Beautiful, listen to the guitar riff at the start, which immediately announces the chorus. Notice how the voices take over from one another line by line in the verses and sing together in the chorus.

artiest/oneohtrix-point-never.text:
Oneohtrix Point Never, abbreviated OPN, is the artist name of Daniel Lopatin, an American electronic producer, composer, singer and songwriter, born on 25 July 1982. He grew up in Massachusetts as the son of Russian-Jewish emigrants with a musical background. His first experiments with electronics grew out of his father's record collection and his father's Roland Juno-60, a synthesizer that he inherited and used extensively in his own music. He studied at Hampshire College and then went to Brooklyn for a course in archival science at the Pratt Institute, a study that also influenced his music.

Lopatin began in the early 2000s in the Brooklyn noise scene. He earned early praise with the synthesizer compilation Rifts from 2009 and with the influential vaporwave project Chuck Person's Eccojams Vol. 1 from 2010. His albums include Returnal in 2010, Replica in 2011, R Plus Seven in 2013, Garden of Delete in 2015, Age Of in 2018, Magic Oneohtrix Point Never in 2020, Again in 2023 and Tranquilizer in 2025. In 2013 he signed with Warp Records. His work uses samples, analogue and software synthesis and intricate MIDI production, and plays with motifs from widely differing genres and eras. He also produced for The Weeknd, Moses Sumney and Soccer Mommy, among others.

Lopatin also wrote film music, above all with the Safdie brothers for Good Time in 2017, Uncut Gems in 2019 and Marty Supreme in 2025. For Good Time he won the Soundtrack Award at the Cannes film festival. OPN shows how electronic music can connect memory, archive and pop.
artiest/oneohtrix-point-never.listen: Listen to a piece from Garden of Delete or Age Of and notice how synthesizer sounds and fragments of other music run together. Ask yourself what you recognise and what you cannot place.

artiest/oneohtrix-point-never-daniel-lop.text: Oneohtrix Point Never is the artist name of Daniel Lopatin, born in Boston in 1982 to Russian-Jewish emigrants with a musical background. The name is a play on the Boston radio station Magic 106.7. He studied archival science at the Pratt Institute in Brooklyn and began in the noise scene of the early 2000s. An important instrument is the Roland Juno-60 synthesizer that he received from his father. With Brian Reitzell he worked on The Bling Ring (2013). For the Safdie brothers he wrote Good Time (2017) and Uncut Gems (2019), and together with Josh Safdie Marty Supreme (2025). Good Time received the Soundtrack Award at Cannes.
artiest/oneohtrix-point-never-daniel-lop.listen: Notice the fast, frantic synthesizer arpeggios and the lack of resting points, which makes the music follow the panic of the protagonists.

artiest/onward-brass-band.text:
The name Onward Brass Band refers to two brass bands that were active in New Orleans for a long time. The first existed from around 1886 to 1930. In its early years it often played at picnics, festivals, parades and baseball games. Around 1887 it was led by cornettist Joseph Othello Lainez and soon became just as popular as the older Excelsior Brass Band and Pickwick Brass Band. After 1903 Manuel Perez took over the leadership. The group usually had ten to twelve players: three cornets or trumpets, two trombones, two clarinets, an alto horn, a baritone horn, a tuba, a snare drum and a bass drum. In the mid-1920s Perez changed the name to Imperial Brass Band. In 1930 the group ceased to exist.

In 1960 Paul Barbarin and Louis Cottrell Jr. revived the name for an ensemble modelled on the old group. Barbarin led it until 1969, then Cottrell. After the latter's death in 1978 Placide Adams took over, until his own death in 2003. In 2005 the band was re-established. It made albums in 1965, 1974 and 2009, and consists of eight to ten players who strictly follow traditional brass band music. Members included Cag Cagnolatti, Kid Howard, Andrew Morgan, Joe Thomas, Louis Barbarin, Alvin Alcorn, Danny Barker and Freddie Kohlman. One recording is Last Journey of a Jazzman: The Funeral of Lester Santiago from 2004.

The Onward Brass Band stands for the music from which jazz in New Orleans grew: parades, funerals and parties, played by wind bands. That the name survived for a century shows how strongly that tradition lives in the city.
artiest/onward-brass-band.listen: Listen to Last Journey of a Jazzman: The Funeral of Lester Santiago and notice the difference between the solemn, slow horns and the lively music that belongs to a New Orleans funeral. Hear how the brass players share the melody.

artiest/opgezwolle.text:
Opgezwolle was a rap group from Zwolle, founded around 1998 by the rappers Sticky Steez, known as Sticks, and Phreako Rico, and DJ and producer Delic. In 2001 the trio won the final of the Oogst van Overijssel, a competition for new talent, and that same year the debut Spuugdingen op de mic was released. The group signed with Top Notch, the label of much Dutch-language hip hop.

The second album, Vloeistof (2003), was released together with an extra record, Brandstof, which could be downloaded for free. Eigen wereld (2006) reached number 4 in the Album Top 100, reportedly the highest position at the time for a Dutch-language rap album. The album came with a film and three videos. Opgezwolle won, among other things, Gouden Grepen for best group (2005) and best album (2006), a 3voor12 Award and a Zilveren Harp. In 2016 voters of Hiphop in je Smoel chose Eigen wereld as the hardest Dutch-language hip hop album of the Low Countries.

Around the group a scene of its own arose in Zwolle. After the solo project Fakkelteit, Opgezwolle stopped around 2007. Rico and Sticks continued in the Fakkelbrigade, with Typhoon among others, who later became known throughout the country. In 2016 they were on stage together again, in a sold-out Heineken Music Hall, followed by a tour. Opgezwolle showed that Dutch hip hop did not have to come only from the big cities in the west.
artiest/opgezwolle.listen: Listen to Hoedenplank, from Eigen wereld (2006), and notice the Dutch of Sticks and Rico: everyday speech, with plenty of internal rhyme. Notice too how the beat underneath keeps itself small, so that the words come first.

artiest/orchestra-dell-accademia-naziona.text:
The Orchestra dell'Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia is an Italian symphony orchestra from Rome. It was founded in 1908 as the first Italian orchestra devoted exclusively to the symphonic repertoire. Today it is based at the Parco della Musica and plays its Roman concerts mainly in the Sala Santa Cecilia. Until 1936 it played in the Anfiteatro Correa, which was built above the Mausoleum of Augustus. Since 1908 the orchestra has given more than fifteen thousand concerts, under conductors including Mahler, Debussy, Strauss, Stravinsky, Sibelius, Toscanini, Furtwängler, Stokowski, Solti, Bernstein, Karajan, Abbado and Morricone.

Bernardino Molinari was the first music director, from 1912 to 1944. He was followed by Franco Ferrara, Fernando Previtali from 1953 to 1973 and Igor Markevitch from 1973 to 1975, among others. In 2005 Antonio Pappano became music director, and with him the orchestra recorded for EMI. He was to end his post in 2023 and receive the title conductor emeritus. In March 2023 Daniel Harding was announced as his successor, from the 2024 to 2025 season.

On record the orchestra is best known for Italian operas: Aïda in 1952, Tosca in 1953 and 1960, Cavalleria rusticana in 1960, later La bohème, Rigoletto, Madama Butterfly, La fanciulla del West, La Traviata and Manon Lescaut. It also recorded Debussy, such as La Mer. The orchestra stands for the Italian opera tradition and thus forms a link to popular music: the melodies of Puccini and Verdi still echo in film music and in pop songs.
artiest/orchestra-dell-accademia-naziona.listen: Listen to an excerpt from La bohème or Tosca in one of the orchestra's recordings and notice how the orchestra supports the singers and underlines their emotion. Hear how the strings sing the melody along with them.

artiest/orchestral-manoeuvres-in-the-dar.text:
Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, OMD for short, is an English electronic band. Andy McCluskey (vocals and bass) and Paul Humphreys (keyboards and vocals) knew each other from primary school in Meols, near Liverpool. As teenagers they played in local bands and discovered Kraftwerk. In 1978 they started OMD together. They chose the long name so that nobody would mistake them for a punk band. They had little money and played on second-hand instruments and home-built equipment. On stage they played along with a tape recorder that they called Winston, after the protagonist of George Orwell's 1984.

Their first single Electricity was released in 1979 on Factory Records, with a sleeve by Peter Saville. Gary Numan took them on tour that same year. With the advance from their new label they built a studio of their own in Liverpool. After the debut Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark (1980) came Organisation, with the anti-war song Enola Gay, which was a hit all over Europe. Architecture & Morality (1981) yielded three hit singles. The experimental Dazzle Ships (1983) was poorly received, after which the band became more accessible with Junk Culture (1984) and broke through in America with If You Leave from the film Pretty in Pink.

OMD combined a bare, experimental approach with pop melodies: synthesizers, drum machines and clear vocal lines. In doing so McCluskey and Humphreys became important founders of synth-pop. After a split and a period with McCluskey alone, they came back together in 2006. Many later electronic acts cite OMD as an example.
artiest/orchestral-manoeuvres-in-the-dar.listen: Listen to Enola Gay from 1980. Notice the cheerful synthesizer melody and the fast drum machine, and how they sound against the lyrics, which are about the atomic bomb on Hiroshima.

artiest/orchestre-al-brihi-de-fes.text:
The Orchestre al-Brihi de Fès is an orchestra from Fez in Morocco that plays Andalusian-Moroccan music, known under the name al-âla. Little is known about the ensemble itself, but its recordings show what it plays: the nuba, a musical form from the Maghreb, found in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya. As the name indicates, it goes back to the music of Al-Andalus. The name nuba comes from the musician's waiting behind a curtain until the curtain man said it was his turn.

According to tradition there were originally twenty-four nubat, one for every hour of the day. A nuba uses one tab' per performance, comparable to a maqam or key, and contains several instrumental pieces and above all sung pieces with accompaniment. The ensemble consists of oud, violins, rabab, nay, qanun, tambourine and darbuka, and the instrumentalists also form the choir. In Morocco there are eleven nubat, which were collected and ordered towards the end of the eighteenth century by the musician Al Haïk of Tetouan. They are so long that a Moroccan nuba is rarely played in full.

The orchestra's recordings make that audible: Nûba Gharîbat Al-Husayn from 1989, and later the complete editions Nûba al-Istihlal from 2012 with a running time of almost eight hours, and nuba al-hijaz al-msharqi from 2014. In this way the orchestra preserves a centuries-old musical memory of the Mediterranean, and is an important source for anyone who wants to hear how Arabic and Spanish music touched one another.
artiest/orchestre-al-brihi-de-fes.listen: Listen to an excerpt from a nuba by this orchestra and notice the alternation between instrumental pieces and sung sections, and the choir of the instrumentalists. Hear how the tempo gradually increases.

artiest/orchestre-lamoureux.text:
The Orchestre Lamoureux is a French symphony orchestra from Paris, founded in 1881 by the violinist and conductor Charles Lamoureux under the name Société des Nouveaux-Concerts. It is one of the oldest orchestral societies in Paris still active, and is also known as the Concerts Lamoureux. For a long time the orchestra gave weekly concerts. After the founder's death it remained an independent organisation, which weathered several financial crises in the twentieth century.

The orchestra played an important role in French musical life. It gave the premières of Chabrier's España in 1883, Fauré's Pavane in 1888, Debussy's Nocturnes in 1900 and 1901 and La mer in 1905, and of Ravel's Menuet antique in 1930 and his Piano Concerto in G in 1932. Its principal conductors included Charles Lamoureux, Camille Chevillard, Paul Paray, Albert Wolff, Eugène Bigot, Jean Martinon, Igor Markevitch and, later, Yutaka Sado and Fayçal Karoui.

On record the orchestra recorded a broad repertoire: Debussy's La mer, Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique, the Carmen and L'Arlésienne Suites by Bizet, Stravinsky Conducts Stravinsky and operettas such as La Périchole and La Belle Hélène. The orchestra stands for a French orchestral sound and for the modern music of around 1900. That makes it important for anyone who wants to understand how the tone colours of Debussy and Ravel found their way into later jazz and film music.
artiest/orchestre-lamoureux.listen: Listen to La mer by Debussy, a work that this orchestra premièred in 1905, and notice how the orchestra evokes waves and colours without a clear melody. Hear how woodwinds and strings are used in layers.

artiest/origa.text:
Origa, born Olga Vitalyevna Yakovleva, was a Russian singer who became known mainly through her collaborations in Japan. She was born on 12 October 1970 in the village of Kochenyovo, fifty kilometres west of Novosibirsk, and died on 17 January 2015. After finishing music school in 1990 she got the chance to visit Japan, and in 1991 she went there. In 1993 she signed with the organisation ROAD&SKY. She worked on various projects with a wide range of artists, sang along in the series of Radio Japan and in the choir of the charity single for the Kobe earthquake. She released eight solo albums, three mini-albums, two compilations and three singles, including ORIGA in 1994, illusia in 1995, Era of Queens in 2003, AURORA in 2005, Amon Ra in 2013 and Lost and Found in 2015.

Outside Japan she became known through Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex and the accompanying soundtrack albums. The music was written by her old friend, the composer Yoko Kanno. Both the title song of the first season, Inner Universe, with boy soprano Ben Del Maestro, and that of the second season, Rise, used her voice. Earlier she had sung the song Moon for ∀ Gundam in concerts with Kanno. In 2005 she sang songs for the anime series Fantastic Children, the best known being the closing theme Mizu no Madoromi, and in 2006 she co-wrote and sang Player and date of rebirth for the film Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex, Solid State Society.

Origa shows how anime music gained a worldwide audience of its own. Her voice, between classical singing and electronics, became a characteristic sound of Yoko Kanno's work.
artiest/origa.listen: Listen to Inner Universe and notice how Origa's voice, together with the boy soprano Ben Del Maestro, creates an almost churchly atmosphere above the electronic accompaniment. Hear how the singing builds towards the chorus.

artiest/original-dixieland-jass-band.text:
The Original Dixieland Jass Band was a band of white musicians from New Orleans that in 1917 released the first jazz record ever. In early 1916 a promoter from Chicago brought a group of New Orleans musicians to his city. After quarrels and changes, the band consisted of Nick LaRocca on cornet, Eddie Edwards on trombone, Larry Shields on clarinet, Henry Ragas on piano and Tony Sbarbaro on drums. Several members had previously played with the New Orleans bandleader Papa Jack Laine. LaRocca and Sbarbaro were children of Sicilian immigrants.

In early 1917 the band played for dancers in a café in New York. On 26 February of that year the group recorded the songs Livery Stable Blues and Dixieland Jass Band One-Step for Victor. The record was released in May and was a surprising success: for many Americans it was their first encounter with jazz. The music was busy and cheerful, with three horns playing in and out of one another at once. At the end of 1917 the band changed the spelling of its name to Jazz. The group also wrote and played standards such as Tiger Rag.

The band called itself the creators of jazz, but that was not true. The music had arisen in the Black community of New Orleans. Even so, the ODJB was the first to put jazz on record and score hits with it, and in this way it helped spread the new music across America. In 1926 the group broke up.
artiest/original-dixieland-jass-band.listen: Listen to Livery Stable Blues and try to hear the animal noises that the horns imitate, such as the neighing of a horse. Notice too how cornet, clarinet and trombone each play their own line at the same time.

artiest/orkest-de-volharding.text:
Orkest de Volharding was a Dutch ensemble for contemporary music from Amsterdam. Louis Andriessen and saxophonist Willem Breuker founded it in 1972, and the name came from Andriessen's work of the same name. The line-up of the first concert, on 12 May 1972, consisted of three trumpets, three saxophones and three trombones, plus Andriessen himself on piano. Flute, horn and bass were then added, and for a time two clarinets as well. This produced the fixed, unusual line-up of one flute, three saxophones, three trumpets, three trombones, a horn and piano.

The original idea was a street orchestra with a political message. Gradually the group grew into a more ordinary ensemble for contemporary music, and in the 1990s it acquired a conductor. Andriessen wrote a number of works for the ensemble before he left in the late 1970s. None of the musicians of the first concert still plays in it, but flautist Dil Engelhard and saxophonist Bob Driessen, who joined immediately after the start, remained members. In 2009 the ensemble ceased to exist. One recording is The Minimalists from 2016.

De Volharding combines the wind instruments of jazz and the wind band with the ideas of the modern Dutch composers. The ensemble showed that contemporary music can also sound with the energy of a street orchestra, and it belongs to the Dutch movement that linked classical, jazz and minimalist music.
artiest/orkest-de-volharding.listen: Listen to a piece from The Minimalists and notice how repeating patterns in saxophones, trumpets and trombones slowly change. Hear how the music recalls both a street orchestra and a jazz band.

artiest/ornette-coleman.text: Ornette Coleman grew up in Fort Worth, Texas, and played rhythm and blues before moving to Los Angeles. Charlie Parker was his starting point, but he wanted to improvise free of fixed chord changes. Many musicians found his playing out of tune. In 1959 he recorded The Shape of Jazz to Come, with Lonely Woman; in November his quartet began at the Five Spot in New York, which divided the jazz world. His album Free Jazz (1960) gave the movement its name. Coleman called his idea harmolodics: harmony, motion and melody are of equal standing. Later he played electric music with Prime Time and in 2007 he won the Pulitzer Prize.
artiest/ornette-coleman.listen: Listen to the melody without a piano beneath it: the bass follows the horns, not the other way round.

artiest/orquesta-america.text:
Orquesta América is a Cuban charanga orchestra founded in Havana in 1942. Singer Ninón Mondéjar started it together with pianist Alex Sosa, the violinists Enrique Jorrín, Antonio Sánchez and Félix Reina, flautist Juan Ramos and others. A charanga is a dance orchestra with, among other things, violins and flute, and it was pre-eminently the sound of the Cuban dance halls in those years. Later Mondéjar and Sosa moved to Mexico and later still to California, where they revived the orchestra.

The most important moment came in 1953. Then the orchestra recorded La Engañadora, a composition by Jorrín, on the Panart label. The record is regarded as the beginning of the cha-cha-chá, a dance and a style that quickly became popular. The success also led to a quarrel: Mondéjar and Jorrín wondered whether the bandleader or the composer deserved the credit for the invention. In December 1954 the orchestra broke up during a tour of Mexico. Juan Ramos returned to Havana with half of the musicians and began Orquesta América del '55 there in 1955. In the 1990s Be Mondéjar took over the leadership. He died in Havana in 2006.

Later albums included Cha cha chá, Charangas, Danzón and Sabor profundo. Orquesta América shows how the cha-cha-chá arose from the charanga tradition, and how a single recording could spread a dance style across the whole world.
artiest/orquesta-america.listen: Listen to La Engañadora. Notice the flute and violins playing the melody, and the calm, constantly recurring rhythm underneath, which you can dance to.

artiest/orquesta-aragon.text:
Orquesta Aragón is a Cuban band that was founded on 30 September 1939 by Orestes Aragón Cantero in Cienfuegos. At first it was called Ritmica 39, then Ritmica Aragón. In the beginning the orchestra consisted of eight musicians: double bass, two violins, piano, flute, timbales, güiro and vocals. When Aragón fell ill in 1949, Rafael Lay Apesteguía took over the leadership. Around 1953 he put the orchestra together according to his own ideas, and flautist Richard Egües, who joined in 1955, became an important arranger and composer, alongside Lay.

Orquesta Aragón did not invent the cha-cha-cha, but in the 1950s and 1960s it was regarded as the best charanga in Cuba. Its trademarks were excellent instrumentalists who played tightly together and rhythmic innovations that kept the sound up to date. The orchestra began as a danzón orchestra and then played cha-cha-cha, onda-cha, pachanga and hybrids with son. Between 1955 and 1958 four LPs appeared on RCA, including That Cuban Cha-Cha-Cha and The Heart of Havana. The onda-cha was an invention of cellist Alejandro Tómas Valdés, who worked capoeira into the dance and let heavy African percussion sound in the cha-cha-cha.

After Lay's death in 1982 Egües became leader, and from 1984 Rafael Lay Bravo. The orchestra still plays in Havana. In the course, El Bodeguero from 1955 is the example of this style. In it we see how Cuban dance music from the halls of Havana travelled out into the world.
artiest/orquesta-aragon.listen: Listen to El Bodeguero. Notice how the flute and violins play tightly together and how light-footed the rhythm underneath stays.

artiest/oscar-brown-jr.text:
Oscar Brown Jr. was an American singer, songwriter, playwright, poet, actor and civil rights activist. He was born on 10 October 1926 in Chicago and died on 29 May 2005. He made his acting debut at fifteen in the Chicago radio programme Secret City. As a young adult he worked as the first Black newsreader in the world for Negro Newsfront, and later he worked in advertising and served in the American army. He ran for the Illinois legislature and for the American House of Representatives, without success. In total he wrote 125 published songs, twelve albums and more than a dozen musical stage plays.

He focused on songwriting when Mahalia Jackson recorded his song Brown Baby. His first major contribution to a record was the collaboration with Max Roach on We Insist! from 1960, one of the first records to celebrate the Black freedom struggle. He then signed with Columbia and released his first album in January 1961, Sin & Soul. It is regarded as a classic because it openly addresses the experiences of African Americans, with songs such as Bid 'Em In and Afro Blue. He also added lyrics of his own to well-known jazz instrumentals, such as Dat Dere, Afro Blue and Work Song, an approach that other jazz singers would follow. Nina Simone later covered his Work Song. Tells It Like It Is from 1963 included The Snake, which in Al Wilson's version became a Northern soul classic. After that his contract with Columbia was not renewed.

Brown shows how jazz and protest found one another: he combined the freedom of jazz with lyrics about Black life in America.
artiest/oscar-brown-jr.listen: Listen to Work Song from Sin & Soul and notice how the lyrics, the singing and the accompaniment evoke the rhythm of labour. Hear how the singing voice almost plays along like an instrument in jazz.

artiest/oscar-hammerstein-ii.text:
Oscar Greeley Clendenning Hammerstein II was an American lyricist, librettist, theatre producer and director, active in the musical for almost forty years. He was born on 12 July 1895 in Harlem, New York, as the grandson of the impresario Oscar Hammerstein I, and died on 23 August 1960. His father managed the Victoria Theatre, but was opposed to his wish to work in the arts. He abandoned his law studies and began as an apprentice to Herbert Stothart, Otto Harbach and Frank Mandel. His first musical, Always You, came to Broadway in 1920. In total he wrote 850 songs and won eight Tony Awards and two Oscars for best song. Many of those songs are standard repertoire for singers and jazz musicians.

With the composer Jerome Kern he wrote Show Boat in 1927, based on the novel by Edna Ferber, which is often revived and regarded as a masterpiece of the American musical. It was a new genre: the musical play, in which the story comes first. He also collaborated with Vincent Youmans, Rudolf Friml and Sigmund Romberg. His longest and most successful collaboration was with Richard Rodgers, which began with Oklahoma! in 1943. Carousel, South Pacific, The King and I, Flower Drum Song and The Sound of Music followed, alongside the film State Fair and the television musical Cinderella. He also wrote the lyrics for Carmen Jones, an adaptation of Bizet's opera Carmen with an all-Black cast.

His pupil Stephen Sondheim called him an experimental playwright. Hammerstein helped bring the American musical to maturity, by putting story and characters at the centre instead of mere light entertainment. From 1956 to 1960 he was president of the Dramatists Guild.
artiest/oscar-hammerstein-ii.listen: Listen to a song from The Sound of Music or Oklahoma! and notice how the lyrics tell a piece of the story and are not just a cheerful tune. Hear how words and melody are matched to each other.

artiest/oscar-holter.text:
Oscar Holter is a Swedish songwriter and producer, born in 1986 in Degerfors. He began in electronic music and played in the Swedish band Necro Facility, which made EBM: hard, danceable electronics. Later he became a writer and producer of pop songs, often together with Max Martin, the Swedish producer behind many of the biggest hits since the 1990s. Holter lives and works in the United States.

His best-known song is Blinding Lights (2019) by The Weeknd, which he wrote and produced together with Max Martin and The Weeknd, for the album After Hours. According to Billboard, the song became the longest-charting hit in the history of the Hot 100. Holter also worked for Taylor Swift, as writer and producer of Dancing With Our Hands Tied (2017), and for Pink, including on Hair Up and Just Like Fire (2016). Katy Perry, Tove Lo, Charli XCX, Carly Rae Jepsen, Troye Sivan and Coldplay are on his list as well.

Holter is an example of how the hit factory works in the 21st century. A song like Blinding Lights has five writers. The star sings and gives the song a face, but behind the scenes a small team of regular writers and producers is at work, a striking proportion of them from Sweden. Their names are in the credits, not on the sleeve, and the general public rarely knows them.
artiest/oscar-holter.listen: In Blinding Lights, listen to the synthesizer riff at the start, which sounds like the 1980s, and to the fast, straight drumbeat. Notice how the riff returns after every chorus and holds the song together.

artiest/oscar-peterson.text:
Oscar Emmanuel Peterson was a Canadian jazz pianist and composer, born on 15 August 1925 in the St. Henri district of Montreal, the son of migrants from the West Indies. He died on 23 December 2007. As a child he played trumpet and piano, but a bout of tuberculosis at the age of seven put an end to the trumpet. His first training was largely classical, with Paul de Marky, a pupil of a pupil of Franz Liszt. Even so, jazz gripped him, especially traditional jazz and boogie-woogie. In 1949 Norman Granz introduced him at a Jazz at the Philharmonic concert in Carnegie Hall, and he remained his manager for almost his whole career.

Peterson recorded more than two hundred records, won eight Grammys and played thousands of concerts over more than sixty years. His trio with bassist Ray Brown and guitarist Herb Ellis, from 1953 to 1958, he himself called the most stimulating. Later came trios with Ray Brown and drummer Ed Thigpen, who recorded Night Train in 1963 and Canadiana Suite in 1965, and in the 1970s with guitarist Joe Pass and bassist Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen. He also played with Ben Webster, Milt Jackson and Herbie Hancock. In 1969 he recorded, on Motions and Emotions, arrangements with orchestra of the Beatles' Yesterday and Eleanor Rigby. His albums about composers, such as Oscar Peterson Plays Cole Porter and Oscar Peterson Plays Duke Ellington, drew attention to the Great American Songbook.

Duke Ellington called him the Maharaja of the keyboard. Peterson is regarded as one of the best jazz pianists and improvisers of the twentieth century, with a virtuosity and a swing that many later pianists took as their yardstick.
artiest/oscar-peterson.listen: Listen to a track from Night Train and notice how piano, bass and drums swing together. Hear how fast Peterson's right hand plays, and how the bass and percussion keep the rhythm tight.

artiest/oscar-pettiford.text:
Oscar Pettiford was an American jazz double bassist and composer, born on 30 September 1922 in Okmulgee, Oklahoma, and died on 8 September 1960. He was one of the first musicians to work in the idiom of bebop. He grew up in the family band, in which he sang and danced, switched to piano at twelve and to double bass at fourteen. The bassist Christian McBride called him probably the most important bassist of the bebop generation, because he created a new language for the bass.

In 1942 he joined the band of Charlie Barnet, and in 1943 he gained wider recognition through his recording of The Man I Love with Coleman Hawkins. In New York in the early 1940s he took part in jam sessions at Minton's Playhouse, where bebop arose, with Dizzy Gillespie, Thelonious Monk and Kenny Clarke, among others. In the 1950s he recorded extensively for Debut, Bethlehem and ABC Paramount, among others, and played on the first three albums that Monk recorded for Riverside. Between 1954 and 1958 he led sextets, big bands and orchestras in Manhattan, in which he sought unusual combinations of sound, such as horns and harp. His composition Tricotism is a standard piece for jazz bass.

Pettiford is also regarded as a pioneer of the cello as a solo instrument in jazz. After breaking his arm in 1949 he could not play his bass and experimented with a cello, which he tuned in fourths, like a double bass, but an octave higher. In 1958 he moved to Copenhagen, where he recorded for European labels, and there he died, just before his thirty-eighth birthday. His influence on later bassists is often mentioned.
artiest/oscar-pettiford.listen: Listen to Tricotism and notice the bass: it plays not only the accompaniment, but also a melodic line of its own. Hear how songlike and nimble the line sounds.

artiest/oslo-philharmonic.text:
The Oslo Philharmonic, in Norwegian Oslo-Filharmonien, is a Norwegian symphony orchestra from Oslo. The orchestra goes back to the Philharmonic Society of 1847 and to the Christiania Musikerforening, co-founded in 1871 by Edvard Grieg and Johan Svendsen. In its present form it has existed since 1919. Since 1977 the orchestra has been based in the Oslo Concert Hall. It gives an average of sixty to seventy symphony concerts a year, most of which are broadcast nationwide on the radio. Since 1934 it has worked closely with the broadcaster NRK. The current principal conductor is Klaus Mäkelä.

The history of the orchestra is closely tied to the theatre. Under Iver Holter it merged with the orchestra of the Christiania Theatre, and from 1889 it received support from the city. In 1899 the Nationaltheatret opened, where the orchestra grew to forty-four musicians under Johan Halvorsen. During the First World War a conflict arose with the theatre, and in 1919 the orchestra was re-established as Filharmonisk Selskaps Orkester, by private shareholders. The first season was shared by the conductors Johan Halvorsen, Georg Schnéevoigt and Ignaz Neumark.

On record the orchestra recorded much Romantic and modern repertoire: symphonies by Tchaikovsky, Mahler and Sibelius, Grieg's Peer Gynt, Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring and Petrushka and Grofé's Grand Canyon Suite from 1959. It is an orchestra that couples its Norwegian roots with the international repertoire, and through its link with the radio it has reached many people.
artiest/oslo-philharmonic.listen: Listen to an excerpt from Peer Gynt: Excerpts from the Incidental Music and notice how the orchestra evokes atmosphere and movement, with strings and woodwinds painting scenes from the play.

artiest/otis-redding.text:
Otis Redding was born in 1941 in Dawson, in the American state of Georgia, and grew up in Macon. He was the greatest star of the soul label Stax in Memphis. The soul of Stax stayed closer to the church and the blues than the polished soul of Motown, and Redding was the face of it.

Redding first sang in the band of guitarist Johnny Jenkins. At Stax he got a contract after an unexpected performance in the studio. His first hit was These Arms of Mine (1962). The house band of Stax, Booker T. & the M.G.'s, with guitarist Steve Cropper, played along with him. The album Otis Blue (1965) includes Respect, which he wrote himself and which Aretha Franklin would turn into a song for women in 1967. His version of Try a Little Tenderness (1966) is regarded as his signature song. In June 1967 he played at the Monterey Pop Festival, for a largely white rock audience. That performance brought him a new audience.

On 10 December 1967 his plane crashed into Lake Monona, near Madison, Wisconsin. Redding was 26. Four members of his backing band The Bar-Kays also died. A few weeks earlier he had recorded (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay with Cropper, a calmer song than his earlier work. It became the first posthumous number 1 single in the American charts and won two Grammys in 1969. In 1989 Redding was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/otis-redding.listen: In (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay (1968), Steve Cropper added the sound of seagulls and waves after Redding's death, as Redding had requested. Listen to the ending too: instead of a last verse, Redding whistles the melody as the song fades away.

artiest/oum-kalthoum.text: Oum Kalthoum learned to sing religious songs from her father as a girl in a village in the Nile Delta and became the greatest female singer of the Arab world in Cairo. From 1934 she gave a concert on the first Thursday of every month that was broadcast live on the radio. In Al-Atlal (1966), to music by Riad Al Sunbati, she sings the same line differently each time, until the hall is swept into ecstasy. At her funeral in 1975 millions of people turned out.
artiest/oum-kalthoum.listen: In Al-Atlal, listen to how the orchestra plays a long introduction before her voice comes in, and how she then bends one phrase again and again.

artiest/oumou-sangare.text: Oumou Sangaré from Bamako is called the songbird of Wassoulou, after the region south of the Niger from which her music comes. Her debut album Moussolou ('women') appeared around 1989 and was an enormous success in West Africa. She sings about love and about the right of women to choose for themselves whom they marry, and she opposes child marriage and polygamy.
artiest/oumou-sangare.listen: Listen to Diaraby Nene: the kamalengoni, a harp with six strings, plays a fast pattern, and the choir answers her singing.

artiest/outkast.text:
OutKast was a hip hop duo from Atlanta, Georgia, formed in 1992 by Antwan Patton (Big Boi) and André Benjamin (André 3000). They met at sixteen in a shopping mall and held rap battles in the canteen of their high school. They chose the name because they dressed differently from their classmates. The local production team Organized Noize took them under its wing, and together with the group Goodie Mob they formed the core of the Dungeon Family.

Their debut Southernplayalisticadillacmuzik (1994) sounded funky, with many live-played instruments, and laid the foundation for Southern hip hop. When the duo received an award in 1995 and was booed by an audience that took only the East and West Coasts seriously, André said that the South had something to say too. ATLiens (1996) and Aquemini (1998) followed, the title of which merges the star signs of the two. On Aquemini, with Rosa Parks, they experimented with funk, soul and real instruments. Stankonia (2000) brought B.O.B. and the number 1 hit Ms. Jackson.

The double album Speakerboxxx/The Love Below (2003) was really two solo albums, one by Big Boi and one by André 3000. It yielded the hits The Way You Move and Hey Ya! and won the Grammy for album of the year. In 2007 they split up. OutKast showed that hip hop from Atlanta could rival New York and Los Angeles, and that rap had room for psychedelia, jazz and humour.
artiest/outkast.listen: Listen to Rosa Parks and notice the acoustic guitar and the hand claps. In the middle section, hear how a harmonica takes over, an instrument you rarely hear in hip hop.

artiest/owen-bradley.text:
William Owen Bradley was an American musician, bandleader and producer, born on 21 October 1915 in Westmoreland, Tennessee, and died on 7 January 1998. Together with Chet Atkins, Bob Ferguson, Bill Porter and Don Law he was one of the most important builders of the Nashville sound in the country and rockabilly of the 1950s and 1960s. In 1935 he got a job at radio station WSM, home of the Grand Ole Opry, and in 1942 he became its music director.

In 1947 the country division of Decca brought him in as an arranger and songwriter. He produced Red Foley's hit Chattanoogie Shoe Shine Boy from 1950 and Kitty Wells' It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels from 1952. In 1954, together with his brother Harold, he built the first studio of what would later become Music Row, in a house in Nashville. Later it became known as the Quonset hut studio. In 1958 he succeeded Paul Cohen as head of Decca in Nashville and began what would come to be called the Nashville sound.

Until then country had been seen as simple and folksy. Bradley and his team of hand-picked musicians, known as the A-Team, gave the melodies more refined lyrics and a polished pop sound. Bradley said that they had left out the fiddle and the steel guitar and added choruses. The singers he produced, such as Kitty Wells, Patsy Cline, Brenda Lee, Loretta Lynn and Conway Twitty, became household names, and rock 'n' roll singers such as Buddy Holly and Gene Vincent also recorded with him.
artiest/owen-bradley.listen: Listen to a record by Patsy Cline and notice how soft the accompaniment is, with choir and strings, and how the vocal stands at the front. Ask yourself what you still recognise as country here.

artiest/ozzy-osbourne.text:
John Michael Ozzy Osbourne was an English singer, songwriter and media personality. He was born on 3 December 1948 in Marston Green, near Birmingham, and died on 22 July 2025. In 1968 he co-founded Black Sabbath, and in the 1970s he became known as their singer. The band is regarded as a pioneer of heavy metal. Osbourne sang on the first eight studio albums, including Black Sabbath and Paranoid in 1970 and Master of Reality in 1971. In 1979 he was fired because of problems with alcohol and other drugs.

In the 1980s he began a solo career, after Ronnie James Dio had replaced him in Black Sabbath. With guitarist Randy Rhoads and bassist Bob Daisley he recorded Blizzard of Ozz in 1980 and Diary of a Madman in 1981. Bark at the Moon in 1983, No More Tears in 1991 and Ordinary Man in 2020 followed, among others. In total he released thirteen solo albums, the first seven of which went multi-platinum in the United States. He reunited with Black Sabbath repeatedly, most recently in 2012, and sang on the last studio album 13 from 2013.

His wife and manager Sharon founded the festival Ozzfest, which ran from 1996 to 2010. In the 2000s he became a television star with the MTV series The Osbournes. In 2006 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of Black Sabbath, and in 2024 as a solo artist as well. His name stands for the birth of heavy metal and for the theatrical rock figure who brought the music to a large audience.
artiest/ozzy-osbourne.listen: Listen to Paranoid by Black Sabbath and notice Ozzy Osbourne's voice against the heavy guitar. Compare that with a song from Blizzard of Ozz and hear how his solo work sounds.

artiest/paavo-berglund.text:
Paavo Allan Engelbert Berglund was a Finnish conductor and violinist, born in Helsinki on 14 April 1929 and died on 25 January 2012. As a child he learned the violin, on an instrument made by his grandfather. At fifteen he knew he wanted to become a musician, and at eighteen he played in restaurants. He studied at the Sibelius Academy in Helsinki and in Vienna and Salzburg. From 1949 to 1958 he was a violinist in the Finnish Radio Symphony Orchestra, where he was the only left-handed player and therefore was given an adapted seat. In Vienna the performance of the Wiener Philharmoniker under Wilhelm Furtwängler made a deep impression on him.

His conducting career began in 1949, when he founded a chamber orchestra of his own, and in 1953 he co-founded the Helsinki Chamber Orchestra. He became known as a strict orchestral disciplinarian, through his relentless rehearsals and his pursuit of perfection. He prepared thoroughly, corrected the parts himself and wrote detailed instructions for every musician. In Britain in 1965 he led the Sibelius commemorative concerts of the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra and became its principal conductor there in 1972, until 1979. In 1979 he also resigned in Helsinki. From 1981 to 1985 he was principal guest conductor of the Scottish National Orchestra. He made more than a hundred recordings, including symphonies by Sibelius and Shostakovich, Finlandia and Smetana's Mein Vaterland.

Berglund conducted all the major North American and European orchestras and was regarded as one of the most important interpreters of Sibelius. His attention to detail and tone colour showed that even familiar symphonies can sound sharp and fresh again.
artiest/paavo-berglund.listen: Listen to Finlandia in his recording and notice the contrasts between the dark, heavy brass at the beginning and the lighter, radiant melody later. Hear how precisely he shapes the dynamics.

artiest/paco-de-lucia.text: Paco de Lucía, born Francisco Sánchez Gómez in Algeciras, named himself after his Portuguese mother Lucía. From 1968 to 1977 he accompanied the singer Camarón de la Isla and in the meantime renewed flamenco guitar. His rumba Entre dos aguas became a hit far beyond the flamenco world. With his sextet he brought the Peruvian cajón into flamenco, and in 1981 he played with John McLaughlin and Al Di Meola.
artiest/paco-de-lucia.listen: Listen to Entre dos aguas and notice the lightning-fast runs, played with alternating index and middle fingers, above a relaxed rumba rhythm.

artiest/pal-waaktaar.text:
Pål Waaktaar, later Paul Waaktaar-Savoy, is the guitarist and main songwriter of the Norwegian pop group a-ha. He was born in 1961 as Pål Gamst in Tonsenhagen, near Oslo; Waaktaar is his mother's family name. As a child he learned to play the flute and studied composition, and he admired Jimi Hendrix. In the late 1970s and early 1980s he was singer, guitarist and writer of the Norwegian rock band Bridges, in which keyboardist Magne Furuholmen also played.

With Furuholmen and singer Morten Harket he formed a-ha in 1982. Waaktaar wrote or co-wrote most of the group's big hits, such as Take On Me, The Sun Always Shines on T.V. and Hunting High and Low, and also the Bond title song The Living Daylights (1987) and the ballad Summer Moved On. His songs combine the sound of synth-pop with broad melodies, which give Harket every room for his high voice. A-ha has sold more than fifty million albums worldwide. In 2012 the three members were made knights of the Order of St. Olav.

Besides a-ha, Waaktaar started the band Savoy, with his wife, the American filmmaker and musician Lauren Savoy, and drummer Frode Unneland. Savoy sold more than 300,000 records in Norway and won three Spellemannprisen, the Norwegian counterpart of the Grammy. Later he worked with singer Jimmy Gnecco in Weathervane and with Gnecco's daughter Zoe in the duo Waaktaar and Zoe. Waaktaar is also a painter and lives in New York and Oslo.
artiest/pal-waaktaar.listen: Listen to the beginning of The Sun Always Shines on T.V.: a calm, floating introduction with Harket's voice, after which the song suddenly bursts open into a big sound of synthesizers and guitar. Notice how Waaktaar built that transition as a dramatic moment.

artiest/palle-danielsson.text:
Nils Paul Palle Danielsson was a Swedish jazz double bassist, born on 15 October 1946 in Stockholm and died on 18 May 2024. His first instrument was the harmonica, which he began playing at the age of two. At eight he played the violin, an instrument he studied for about five years. During that time he became interested in jazz and began playing double bass. At fifteen he was already playing professionally. He studied from 1962 to 1966 at the Royal Academy of Music in Stockholm and then played with Scandinavian musicians such as Eje Thelin, Bobo Stenson and Jan Garbarek, and in international collaborations with, among others, Lee Konitz and Steve Kuhn.

From 1974 to 1979 he was a member of Keith Jarrett's quartet. His albums from that time include Belonging from 1974. He further worked with Bill Evans, Kenny Wheeler, Geri Allen, Michel Petrucciani, Charles Lloyd, Peter Erskine, Elvin Jones, Ben Webster, George Russell, Albert Mangelsdorff, Enrico Rava, Tomasz Stańko and John Taylor. In Sweden he also led groups himself and released several recordings, such as Giulia's Thursdays in 2012 and Breathing In Unison in 2014.

Danielsson shows that Scandinavian jazz had a spacious sound of its own. His bass was a steady, warm ground beneath the improvisations of great names, and he connected European and American jazz. He is an example of the bassist as a load-bearing force in a band, not as a soloist in the foreground.
artiest/palle-danielsson.listen: Listen to Belonging by Keith Jarrett's quartet and notice the bass beneath piano and saxophone: how calm and yet present Danielsson remains. Hear how he fills the space between the soloists.

artiest/pandit-jasraj.text:
Pandit Jasraj was an Indian classical singer from the Mewati gharana, a musical lineage. He was born on 28 January 1930 in the village of Pili Mandori in Haryana, into a family of classical singers, and died on 17 August 2020. His father Motiram died in 1934 when he was four, and his eldest brother Maniram taught him. He grew up in Hyderabad and often travelled to Sanand in Gujarat to take lessons from musicians of the Mewati gharana. In 1946 he moved to Calcutta, where he began singing classical music on the radio.

At first he learned to play the tabla and accompanied his brother. At fourteen he began to focus on singing, after he had given up the tabla because of the way accompanists were treated. He practised about fourteen hours a day. In 1952, aged twenty-two, he gave his first concert as a singer at the court of King Tribhuvan in Kathmandu. His career spanned seventy-five years. He sang classical, semi-classical and devotional music, recorded albums and film music, such as Baiju Bawra, and taught in India, Europe, Canada and the United States. He gave new life to the Mewati gharana and renewed genres such as the Haveli Sangeet.

He sang khayals with a certain freedom and added elements of lighter styles, such as the thumri. For this he was criticised at first. He also created a new form of jugalbandi, Jasrangi, in which a man and a woman simultaneously sing different ragas. He was also known for rare ragas such as Abiri Todi and Patdeepaki. In this way he showed how a centuries-old tradition stays alive.
artiest/pandit-jasraj.listen: Listen to a raga from Morning to Midnight Ragas and notice how his voice slowly opens and stretches and ornaments every note. Hear how the mood of the raga is built up step by step.

artiest/panjabi-mc.text:
Panjabi MC is the artist name of Rajinder Singh Rai, a British rapper, producer and DJ. He was born in 1973 in Coventry, to parents from the Indian state of Punjab. His name comes from the Punjabi that he raps and spins in his music. His aim is to bring bhangra and hip hop together, two worlds that he knows well. He got a contract with Nachural Records after he had made a remix of Ghariah Milan De, a song by Kuldeep Manak.

His first successful record was Mundian To Bach Ke, in Punjabi Beware of the Boys. The song was on the 1998 album Legalised. It combines bhangra with the recognisable bass line from the television series Knight Rider. At first it was an underground hit on the internet. Then the German label Superstar Recordings picked it up, and in 2002 it became a big hit in Europe, including in Germany and Britain. In 2003 a version with the American rapper Jay-Z appeared. In the same year Jogi came out. His early singles and the Jay-Z version brought bhangra to a worldwide audience via the BBC. Later came, among others, Indian Timing (2008), on which he used a vocal sample by Ofra Haza, and 56 Districts (2019).

AllMusic called him one of the best-known names in bhangra. His work shows how the music of the Punjabi community in Britain won a place of its own in world pop, by mixing traditions with hip hop and television music.
artiest/panjabi-mc.listen: Listen to Mundian To Bach Ke. Notice the dhol and the Punjabi singing, and the bass line that you may recognise from the television series Knight Rider.

artiest/paris-grey.text:
Paris Grey is an American singer, born in 1965 in Glencoe, near Chicago. She was the original singer of Inner City, the group that producer Kevin Saunderson started in Detroit in 1987. Saunderson was, together with Juan Atkins and Derrick May, one of the Belleville Three, the founders of Detroit techno. With Inner City he brought that machine-made dance music together with pop vocals, and Grey supplied the voice.

The first big success was Big Fun (1988), which reached number 8 in England and was number 1 on the American dance chart. Good Life followed, which reached number 4 in England, and in 1989 Ain't Nobody Better and Do You Love What You Feel. In total Inner City was number 1 on the American dance chart five times and had nine hits in the British top 40. The album Paradise (1989), called Big Fun in America, reached number 3 in England and went platinum there.

Inner City made techno suitable for the hit parade. The music remained built on drum machines, synthesizers and tight repetition, but with Grey's singing it acquired a chorus to sing along to. In this way Detroit techno, which began as music for clubs, also became music for the radio and the charts, especially in England. About Grey's later life the sources say little.
artiest/paris-grey.listen: In Big Fun, listen to the contrast between the cool, mechanical beat and Paris Grey's singing, which turns it into a singalong. Notice the synthesizer chords that keep returning and give the song a cheerful colour.
